strengths: The paper addresses a significant challenge in whole-body control (WBC) for humanoid robotics: sample inefficiency during reinforcement learning.

The core idea of leveraging privileged simulator states alongside zero-masked proprioceptive states as natural contrastive pairs (PvP) avoids hand-crafted heuristic augmentations (e.g., noise injection) that might distort physical dynamics.

The authors introduce SRL4Humanoid, providing a modular framework that benchmarks representative state representation learning (SRL) paradigms (contrastive, predictive/dynamics modeling, and reconstruction) on humanoid WBC.

The empirical analysis includes insightful ablation studies regarding update frequency, data proportion, and applying SRL to policy versus value encoders, offering actionable insights for training complex humanoid policies.
weaknesses: Missing comparisons with standard privileged learning paradigms: The predominant way privileged simulator information is transferred to proprioceptive policies in legged and humanoid robotics is via teacher-student policy distillation or system identification/adaptation modules (e.g., RMA, CTS, or concurrent adaptation networks). The paper only benchmarks against auxiliary SRL baselines (VAE, SPR, SimSiam) rather than established privileged-to-proprioceptive distillation approaches.

Architectural ad-hoc design: To align dimensions for the shared-weight encoder, the proprioceptive state is permanently zero-padded to match the privileged state dimension during both training and deployment. The implications of this zero-padding and whether an asymmetric dual-encoder architecture would be more effective are not deeply explored.

Limited real-world quantitative evaluation: The real-robot experiment on the LimX Oli humanoid is discussed only superficially (Figure 1c and a short mention in Section 5.2.6) without quantitative metrics, tracking errors, success rates, or comparative physical performance against baselines.

Relevance to computer vision: The framework operates entirely on low-dimensional proprioceptive and kinematic states (joint angles, velocities, base poses) without any visual or sensory perception (RGB/depth images, elevation maps, point clouds). While embodied control is increasingly featured at vision conferences, the absence of visual representation learning makes the venue fit questionable.

strengths: The core idea of PvP is intuitive and elegant: using SimSiam-style contrastive learning between the full privileged state and a zero-masked proprioceptive state avoids the need for ad-hoc heuristic data augmentations while naturally distilling privileged simulator information into the policy encoder.
The paper introduces SRL4Humanoid, a modular and unified benchmarking platform integrating multiple state representation learning paradigms (VAE, SPR, SimSiam, PvP) for humanoid whole-body control.

The empirical analysis is thorough regarding training dynamics, offering useful practical insights such as the effect of update intervals (avoiding collapse from early low-quality data), rollout data proportions, and applying SRL to the policy versus value encoder.

The method is demonstrated on a challenging 31-DoF humanoid platform (LimX Oli) across both velocity tracking and motion imitation tasks, including Sim2Sim verification in MuJoCo and real-robot hardware demonstration.
weaknesses: From a methodological standpoint, the novelty is somewhat incremental. PvP is essentially SimSiam applied directly to a state vector and its zero-masked counterpart, acting as an auxiliary loss alongside asymmetric PPO.

Comparison against established privileged learning baselines is incomplete. In legged and humanoid robotics, the standard ways to exploit privileged simulator information are auxiliary regression (e.g., directly predicting linear root velocity or terrain height from proprioceptive history via MSE) and teacher-student / RMA-style distillation. The baselines compared here are generic SRL methods (VAE, SPR, SimSiam), omitting a direct comparison against standard privileged auxiliary prediction or distillation.

Technical clarity regarding input dimensionality at inference time could be improved: the paper indicates that $\tilde{s}_t = \text{ZeroMasking}(s_t)$ has the same dimensionality as $s_t$, but typical deployment policies take only proprioception $o_t$. Clarifying whether the network permanently expects zero-padded vectors or has modality-specific input projections would improve reproducibility.

The real-robot deployment evaluation is purely qualitative and brief (a photographic snapshot in Figure 1 and a brief mention in Section 5.2.6). There are no quantitative real-world comparisons (e.g., tracking error, fall rate, push recovery) comparing PvP to baseline controllers on physical hardware.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in humanoid robotics: improving sample efficiency and whole-body control (WBC) stability in reinforcement learning.

The proposed method, PvP, is simple and conceptually clean, utilizing a SimSiam-style contrastive objective between full privileged simulator states and zero-masked proprioceptive states without requiring handcrafted augmentations.

Comprehensive empirical analysis covering multiple training dynamics questions, such as the effect of update intervals, rollout data subsampling proportions, and applying representation learning to the policy vs. value encoder.
Includes physical hardware validation and Sim2Sim deployment on the 31-DoF LimX Oli humanoid robot.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The core contribution is largely an adaptation of SimSiam to structured state vectors by treating the zero-masked state as a paired view, which represents an incremental algorithmic advance.

Missing comparison with standard privileged information baselines: Humanoid locomotion and whole-body control literature heavily relies on teacher-student distillation or explicit supervised privileged estimation (e.g., Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) or concurrent teacher-student learning (CTS)). The paper critiques regression-based privileged reconstruction in Section 4.1 but only benchmarks against an unsupervised VAE reconstructing proprioceptive observations, leaving standard supervised privileged estimators uncompared.

Lack of quantitative real-world evaluations: While real-robot deployment on the LimX Oli is highlighted, Section 5.2.6 presents purely qualitative visual snapshots and references video demonstrations. Quantitative comparisons against baselines (e.g., tracking RMSE, success rates, fall rates, or disturbance rejection) in Sim2Sim and real hardware are absent.

Scope and relevance: The methodology operates strictly on low-dimensional proprioceptive and privileged kinematic/dynamic vectors with no visual perception, depth, or point cloud inputs, making its fit for a computer vision conference relatively marginal compared to robotics venues.

strengths: Simple and effective formulation: PvP leverages the intrinsic relationship between privileged simulator states and proprioceptive states via a SimSiam-style contrastive loss with zero-masking, avoiding the need for hand-crafted data augmentations in state-based RL.

Comprehensive empirical investigation: The paper conducts systematic ablations addressing key operational questions, such as the effect of update intervals (finding periodic updates help prevent early collapse), data subsampling ratios, and applying SRL to policy vs. value encoders.

Release of SRL4Humanoid: Providing a unified, modular open-source framework implementing multiple SRL baselines (SimSiam, SPR, VAE) tailored for humanoid whole-body control is a valuable practical contribution to the community.

Validation across multiple tasks and hardware: Evaluated on high-DoF humanoid platforms (LimX Oli 31 DoF and Unitree G1 29 DoF) across velocity tracking and motion imitation tasks, including Sim2Sim and physical hardware deployment.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The core technical novelty is relatively incremental, essentially adapting standard SimSiam to low-dimensional vector states by zero-masking privileged features as an augmentation. The conceptual step beyond existing asymmetric actor-critic or latent state matching is modest.

Absence of quantitative real-world evaluation: While real-world deployment on the LimX Oli robot is presented qualitatively in Figure 1 and referenced in supplementary videos, there are no quantitative real-world metrics (e.g., tracking error, success rates over repeated runs, push-recovery or terrain disturbance tests) to substantiate sim-to-real transfer claims.

Domain fit and lack of perceptual inputs: The state representation learning in this paper operates exclusively over low-dimensional kinematic/dynamic state vectors (e.g., joint velocities, base velocities, orientation). Given the CVPR venue, the lack of visual modalities (e.g., RGB, depth, elevation heightmaps) weakens its direct relevance to the computer vision community.

Teacher-Student Distillation (TSD) baseline comparison: In Appendix D.1, the student in the TSD baseline performs drastically worse than the teacher. Further analysis or tuning of distillation schemes (e.g., temporal history encoders as in RMA) is needed to ensure the baseline is fairly optimized.

strengths: Clear motivation and practical relevance: Addressing sample inefficiency and partial observability in humanoid whole-body control (WBC) is a critical challenge in embodied AI and robotics.

Simple yet effective methodology: Using privileged simulator states and their zero-masked proprioceptive counterparts as views for self-supervised contrastive learning (SimSiam-style) avoids the need for ad-hoc, hand-crafted data augmentations.

Valuable system/benchmark contribution: The introduction of the modular 'SRL4Humanoid' framework systematically benchmarked against representative state representation learning paradigms (reconstruction via VAE, dynamics modeling via SPR, and self-supervised contrastive learning via SimSiam) provides a useful foundation for reproducible research.

Comprehensive empirical investigation: The paper thoroughly ablates training update intervals, data proportions, policy vs. value encoder placement, loss weighting coefficients, and demonstrates improvements across multiple robot embodiments (LimX Oli, Unitree G1) and terrain conditions.
Sim2Sim and hardware validation: The policy is successfully transferred to MuJoCo simulation and deployed on a real LimX Oli humanoid robot.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The algorithmic contribution primarily adapts standard SimSiam negative-cosine similarity with stop-gradients to the difference between privileged and masked proprioceptive state vectors. While effective, the novelty from a representation learning standpoint is somewhat limited.

Lack of representation probing / qualitative latent analysis: The paper claims that PvP captures compact and task-relevant dynamics without reconstructing noise, but does not provide diagnostic analyses (e.g., linear probing of unobserved privileged states like base linear velocity, singular value spectrum analysis to assess dimensional collapse, or t-SNE visualizations) to empirically substantiate what the learned latent space captures.

Lack of quantitative real-world evaluation: Section 5.2.6 presents real-robot testing solely through qualitative video snapshots (Figure 1c). Providing quantitative metrics on hardware (such as velocity tracking RMSE, gait stability, push-recovery resistance, or success rates) compared to vanilla PPO would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

Clarity on dimension handling and architecture during deployment: While Appendix C.2 notes that zero-masking is appended to the proprioceptive state to match dimensions, the main text (Section 4.1) leaves ambiguities regarding how history stacking (e.g., 5 frames for proprioception vs. 1 frame for privileged state in Table 2) interacts with weight sharing between $f_\theta(s)$ and $f_\theta(\tilde{s})$.

strengths: The proposed PvP framework introduces an intuitive and elegant concept: treating the privileged state and the zero-masked privileged state (proprioception) as natural multi-view pairs for contrastive learning, circumventing the need for heuristic data augmentation in robotic continuous state spaces.

The paper provides an extensive empirical study through the modular SRL4Humanoid framework, systematically comparing representative SRL paradigms (reconstruction via VAE, predictive modeling via SPR, and contrastive learning via SimSiam) alongside thorough ablations on update intervals, data proportions, and encoder placement.

Strong experimental evaluation across diverse scenarios (velocity tracking, motion imitation, and rough terrain) and two humanoid platforms (LimX Oli and Unitree G1), supplemented by Sim2Sim validation in MuJoCo and physical deployment on the real LimX Oli robot.
weaknesses: Relevance to computer vision: The framework operates purely on low-dimensional state vectors (joint positions, velocities, orientations, base linear velocities) without visual observations (such as RGB or depth images). While representation learning for embodied systems falls broadly under pattern recognition, the lack of visual perception somewhat limits its topical alignment with CVPR.

Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: The algorithmic core directly adopts SimSiam with a stop-gradient cosine similarity loss, where the 'augmentation' is zero-masking privileged features. The technical novelty lies mainly in the empirical application and formulation rather than new representation learning fundamentals.

Clarification on observation space alignment: In Table 2 and Section 4.1, the privileged and proprioceptive states appear to have different shapes (e.g., stacked history $3 	imes 5$ for proprioception vs. instantaneous base linear velocity for privileged state). The manuscript could more clearly explain how zero-masking is structured during deployment to ensure that the policy encoder only relies on real-time available proprioceptive history without dimensional discrepancies.
